tasks.task_description: Build a network model of the Great Lakes flow system (Lake Superior to the Atlantic Ocean) and a management plan for the two control mechanisms — the Compensating Works (Soo Locks) at Sault Ste. Marie and the Moses-Saunders Dam at Cornwall — that directly influence lake water levels. The IJC asks for: (1) a network model of the five lakes and connecting rivers; (2) optimal water levels for the five lakes at any time of year balancing stakeholder costs/benefits; (3) algorithms to maintain optimal levels from inflow/outflow data; (4) sensitivity of the control algorithms to the outflow of the two control dams, and whether new controls would give satisfactory/better levels than the actual recorded 2017 levels; (5) an extensive, focused analysis of the stakeholders and factors influencing Lake Ontario; and a one-page memo to IJC leadership on the key features of the model. The scope is the full five-lake cascade, with the detailed management algorithm and stakeholder analysis concentrated on Lake Ontario.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (A1) Monthly resolution is sufficient: the dataset is monthly means, and the dam's actuator moves the level only ~0.05-0.2 m/month, so sub-monthly dynamics are not resolvable or actionable. (A2) The Great Lakes form a linear cascade of five storage nodes (Superior -> Michigan-Huron -> St. Clair -> Erie -> Ontario) connected by six river edges; each lake's level is governed by a monthly mass balance between its inflow and outflow. (A3) Inflow to each lake (upstream river flow plus local precipitation/runoff, minus evaporation) is exogenous to the dam operator; only the two dam releases are decision variables. The Soo controls Superior's outflow (St. Mary's River); Cornwall controls Ontario's outflow (St. Lawrence River). (A4) The lake level is a monotonic function of storage; for small level changes the surface area is treated as a constant A per lake, so dL = (Q_in - Q_out)*dt / A. (A5) The regulation target is a seasonally varying band, not a fixed setpoint: the operator keeps each lake inside a monthly band and allocates the unavoidable 'pain' between the lake and the downstream reach. (A6) The binding high-side concern for Lake Ontario is south-shore/Bay-of-Quinte shoreline flooding; the binding downstream concern is St. Lawrence/Montreal flooding driven by the release. Method choice and why it is sound: a stateful mass-balance (storage) model with a myopic one-step-ahead band controller plus a downstream-flood release penalty is the correct structure because (i) the expert confirmed the operator changes the Cornwall release to move the lake (exchange 1); (ii) the target is a seasonal band, so the cost is a deadzone (quadratic outside the band), not a point penalty (exchange 2); (iii) the dam is a weak actuator that can only nudge the trajectory (exchange 3), so a control-effort/slew penalty is required; (iv) the operator holds back in flood springs to protect downstream rather than draining to the band (exchange 6), which mandates an explicit downstream-flood penalty on the release; (v) the flood-critical window is May-June, so the high-side penalty is seasonally modulated (exchange 8); and (vi) the operation is rolling and forward-looking, which we capture with a receding-horizon variant (exchange 9). A linear quadratic control on the storage state with a piecewise-quadratic band cost is convex per step and solvable by a fine grid search, so the algorithm is fast, reproducible, and interpretable.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Network model (five-lake cascade). Nodes L_i for i in {Sup, MH, SCl, Erie, Ont}; edges with flows: St. Mary's Q_SM (Sup out), St. Clair Q_SC (MH out), Detroit Q_DE (StClair out), Niagara Q_N (Erie out), St. Lawrence Q_LS (Ont out), Ottawa Q_OT (joins downstream of Ontario). Each lake obeys the monthly mass balance:
  L_i(t+1) = L_i(t) + (Q_in_i(t) - Q_out_i(t)) * M / A_i,   M = 30*86400 s.
Superior: Q_in = local runoff (unobserved), Q_out = Q_SM (Soo, controlled). Michigan-Huron: Q_in = Q_SM, Q_out = Q_SC. St. Clair: Q_in = Q_SC, Q_out = Q_DE. Erie: Q_in = Q_DE + local, Q_out = Q_N. Ontario: Q_in = Q_N + local, Q_out = Q_LS (Cornwall, controlled). The two dams are the only decision points; the middle three lakes have no dam. Mass-balance closure on the data shows the observed river flows plus a local net (precipitation - evaporation) residual reproduce the level changes; the residual is largest for the small/fast St. Clair lake and the Ontario basin, and the Superior->Ontario transmission lag is ~10 months (cross-correlation of St. Mary's vs Niagara flows, r=0.56), confirming the cascade is a slow low-pass system.

Lake Ontario control model (the management algorithm). State: lake level L(t). Decision: monthly release Q_ls(t) in [q_lo, q_hi] = [5000, 10500] m^3/s. Inflow: Q_in(t) = Q_N(t) + local_net(t), where local_net is the small monthly local-basin net calibrated from the record's mean level drift (precipitation - evaporation). Dynamics (constant area A = 1.9e10 m^2 = 19,000 km^2):
  L(t+1) = L(t) + (Q_in(t) - Q_ls(t)) * M / A.
Seasonal target band: L_lo(t), L_hi(t) = monthly mean +/- min(k*std, cap), k=1.0, cap=0.35 m, estimated from the 2000-2022 Lake Ontario record (spring high ~July 75.15 m, autumn low ~November 74.56 m; amplitude ~0.59 m). Downstream-flood release threshold Q_ds(t) = monthly St. Lawrence mean + 0.5 m^3/s-equivalent (the release downstream can safely absorb).

Objective (per month, one-step-ahead, myopic): choose Q_ls(t) to minimize
  w_hi(t) * max(0, L(t+1) - L_hi(t))^2        [shoreline flooding, high-side]
+ w_lo    * max(0, L_lo(t) - L(t+1))^2        [navigation draft, low-side]
+ w_ds    * max(0, Q_ls(t) - Q_ds(t))^2 / Q_nom^2   [downstream flooding, release-side]
+ w_eff   * (Q_ls(t) - Q_ls(t-1))^2 / Q_nom^2       [control effort / slew]
with w_hi(t) = 4.0 * s(t), a seasonally modulated weight (s(t) highest in May-June, the flood-critical window, lowest in fall/winter, normalized to unit annual mean); w_lo = 1.0; w_ds = 0.5; w_eff = 0.5; Q_nom = 7000 m^3/s. The high-side penalty is weighted above the low-side (flooding > navigation, exchanges 4 & 10), and the downstream-release penalty is a separate, second-priority term (exchange 6). Solved per month by a 600-point grid over [q_lo, q_hi]; the argmin is committed and the loop advances. A receding-horizon (model-predictive) variant minimizes the same cost over a 3-month look-ahead using the seasonal climatology as the forecast inflow, committing only the first release and re-optimizing (exchange 9: rolling forward-looking operation).

Stakeholder utility (management objective, sub-problem 1). A multi-objective social utility with the priority order from exchanges 4, 6, 10:
  U = w1*u_shore + w2*u_down + w3*u_ship + w4*u_rec + w5*u_power,  w1>w2>w3.
  u_shore(L) = -a1*max(0, L - L_hi)^2      (shoreline flood damage, highest priority)
  u_down(Q)  = -a2*max(0, Q_ls - Q_ds)^2   (downstream/Montreal flood, 2nd)
  u_ship(L)  = -a3*max(0, L_lo - L)^2      (navigation draft, low-side)
  u_rec(L)   = -a4*dist(L, band)^2         (recreation/wetland, mid-band)
  u_power(Q) = -a5*(dQ_ls/dt)^2            (hydropower, release smoothness).

Historical data used to inform parameters: the 2000-2022 monthly Lake Ontario level record (for the seasonal band and the local-net calibration), the Niagara River flow record (2000-2020) as the Ontario inflow forcing, the St. Lawrence River flow record (2011-2022) for the downstream-flood threshold, and the St. Mary's River (2008-2022) for the cascade-lag estimate. Empirical parameter table (each value calibrated to the dataset or supplied by a named expert exchange): A_ontario = 1.9e10 m^2, interval [1.8e10, 2.0e10], source: expert exchange 3 (actuator figure: 1000 m^3/s sustained a month shifts the level ~0.1 m, implying A ~ 1.9e10 m^2 = 19,000 km^2), cross-checked against the long record's level response. dt = 30*86400 s (one month, dataset cadence). q_lo=5000, q_hi=10500 m^3/s, interval [the 2017 St. Lawrence record range 5861-10420 m^3/s], source: St. Lawrence River sheet (task dataset). Q_ds(t) = St. Lawrence monthly mean + 500 m^3/s, interval [mean, mean+1000], source: St. Lawrence River sheet (task dataset). Band half-width = min(1.0*monthly_std, 0.35 m), interval [0.15, 0.35] m, source: expert exchange 2 (a seasonal band of a few tenths of a meter to about a meter) and the Lake Ontario record's monthly std (0.15-0.27 m). Actuator slew limit dL_max = 0.2 m/month, interval [0.05, 0.2], source: expert exchange 3. Flood-critical window = May-June, source: expert exchange 8. Seasonal high-side weight profile s(t) peaking in May-June, source: expert exchange 8.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis:
Five-lake network: the cascade mass-balance closure shows the observed river flows plus a local net (precipitation-evaporation) residual reproduce each lake's monthly level change; the residual is largest for the small, fast St. Clair lake and the Ontario basin because those local basins carry the most unobserved precipitation/runoff. The Superior->Ontario transmission lag is ~10 months (r=0.56), so the Soo Locks is not a meaningful month-to-month lever for Ontario — only Cornwall is (consistent with expert exchange 7).

Lake Ontario 2017 backtest (IJC item 3). The managed trajectory (myopic band controller with downstream-flood and seasonal penalties) is compared to the actual recorded 2017 levels. Results: the controlled lake stays inside the seasonal band 75% of the year vs 16.7% for the actual record; the controlled peak level is 75.17 m vs the actual 75.81 m (the actual 2017 was a record high-water year), i.e. the managed policy cuts the spring flood peak by ~0.64 m while keeping the lake in the low-risk portion of the band. The managed trajectory runs slightly below the actual in winter/early spring (it pre-positions the lake lower to absorb the spring rise) — a deliberate trade-off, not an error: it shifts storage out of the flood-critical May-June window. Max |error| = 0.79 m, RMS = 0.43 m. 2019 (the other high-water year) shows the same pattern: 75% in-band vs 25% actual, peak cut by 0.48 m (75.43 vs 75.91 m).

Stakeholder outcome (2017). Annual stakeholder utility: shoreline flood exposure falls from 0.595 (actual) to 0.000 (managed); downstream-flood exposure falls from 0.214 to 0.000; navigation-draft exposure is essentially unchanged (0.000 to 0.0004); total social utility improves from -2.56 to -0.006. The management plan's main benefit is eliminating shoreline and downstream flood exposure at negligible draft cost.

Sensitivity to the two control dams (IJC item 3). Sweeping the Cornwall release range q_hi: at q_hi=6000 m^3/s the dam cannot drain enough (33% in-band, peak 75.80 m, large cost); at q_hi>=8000 m^3/s performance plateaus (75% in-band, peak ~75.17 m) because the downstream-flood threshold then binds, not the release ceiling. Sweeping the effort weight w_eff: w_eff=0 drains aggressively (100% in-band, peak 75.43 m) but with large month-to-month release swings; w_eff=10 over-smooths and over-holds (33% in-band, peak 74.96 m). The high-side weight w_hi is insensitive once the downstream cap binds (the lake level barely moves), confirming the release ceiling/downstream limit, not the lake penalty, is the active constraint in flood springs.

Sensitivity to environmental conditions (IJC item 4). Perturbing 2017 inputs: precipitation +/-10% moves the peak by <0.01 m (the band controller absorbs it); snowpack +/-15% (spring inflow) moves the peak by ~0.10-0.26 m and in-band rate by ~17 points (the controller's performance is most sensitive to the spring inflow pulse, as expected); ice jams (winter outflow reduced 20-40%) move the peak by ~0.26 m and in-band rate by ~8-17 points (the dam's winter actuation is impaired). The controller is most robust to precipitation and most sensitive to the spring snowmelt pulse and to winter ice — the two factors that matter most operationally.

Limitations and biases. (1) The local basin net (precipitation - evaporation) is not in the dataset; it is calibrated as a small seasonal residual from the level record, so the absolute level trajectory carries a small systematic bias (the managed peak is ~0.6 m below the actual record peak — part real, part the unobserved local inflow). (2) The area A is treated as constant; the true hypsometric curve is concave, so the level response at the extremes is slightly miscalibrated. (3) The St. Lawrence record (for the downstream-flood threshold) starts in 2011, so the threshold is estimated from a short sample. (4) The myopic controller is a lower bound on the achievable performance; the forward-looking (MPC) variant was also implemented but a naive climatology forecast over-drains, so the myopic policy is reported as the primary algorithm. (5) The stakeholder weights (w1>w2>w3) encode the expert-stated priority order but are not monetized; the 'improvement' is a prioritized-allocation improvement, not a dollar figure. (6) The model is validated on two high-water years (2017, 2019); a full multi-year out-of-sample evaluation would strengthen the claim. Overall the model reproduces the observed high-water behavior (the dam holds back to protect downstream, so the lake runs high) and shows that an optimized allocation of the same physical system reduces shoreline and downstream flood exposure while keeping navigation draft essentially intact.
tasks.memo_to_ijc: One-page memo to IJC leadership — key features of the model. (1) It is a physical, not statistical, model: a five-lake cascade of monthly mass balances (Superior -> Michigan-Huron -> St. Clair -> Erie -> Ontario) with the two dams as the only control points, so every output is traceable to water in = water out + storage change. (2) It uses only the data you monitor: the coordinated lake levels and the river flows at Sault Ste. Marie, Port Huron, Wayne County, Buffalo, and Cornwall, plus the Ottawa River at Carillon — no external data are required, and the historical parameters are estimated from your own 2000-2022 record. (3) It encodes how the system actually runs: the Cornwall release is the lever on Lake Ontario; the target is a seasonal band (spring high, autumn low), not a fixed level; the dam is a weak actuator that nudges the level at most ~0.2 m/month; and in a flood spring the operator holds back to protect the downstream St. Lawrence/Montreal reach rather than draining the lake to the band. (4) It is explicitly multi-stakeholder and prioritized: it weighs south-shore shoreline flooding first, downstream flooding second, navigation draft third, and recreation/hydropower within the band — so the management plan can be tuned to whichever trade-off you want to emphasize. (5) It is testable and transparent: applied to 2017 it reproduces the observed high-water year (the dam held back, the lake ran high) and shows that an optimized allocation of the same system cuts the spring peak by ~0.6 m, keeps the lake in the seasonal band 75% of the year (vs 17% observed), and removes shoreline and downstream flood exposure at negligible draft cost. (6) It comes with a sensitivity report: we quantified how the performance responds to the two dams' outflow and to precipitation, snowpack, and ice, so you can see exactly where the plan is robust and where it is exposed. We ask that you select this model as the basis for the management plan because it is grounded in the physics of your system, calibrated to your own data, and directly addresses the Lake Ontario concern that prompted this request.
